reception.text: The Caucasian of Clinton, North Carolina, summarized the proclamation's orders on its front page, beside a report of King Edward VII's cabled sympathy.
Hay's death was front-page news; the Raleigh Morning Post led with "HAY'S BODY LAID TO REST," describing Roosevelt standing "close to the open grave."
The Norfolk Virginian-Pilot, a Democratic daily, praised Hay as the country's first citizen and a patriot of the opposite party, while taking a jab at the administration's style.
The same page reprinted a New Orleans States tribute ranking Hay a great diplomat and a statesman of high ability.

political_impact.text: The proclamation followed a fixed precedent, Grover Cleveland's 1895 proclamation for Secretary of State Walter Q. Gresham, and nothing found suggests it drew controversy.
Roosevelt named Elihu Root, his former Secretary of War, to succeed Hay; Root entered on duty July 19, 1905.
political_impact.source: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian

legacy.text: Hay is remembered chiefly for the Open Door policy toward China and for the treaties that made the Panama Canal legally possible; his name survives in the Hay–Pauncefote and Hay–Bunau-Varilla treaties.
Roosevelt's death proclamations did not share one fixed form; each borrowed from whatever precedent fit the case.

related.note: Roosevelt's proclamation on the death of William McKinley, which set a day of mourning and prayer.
Roosevelt's proclamation on the death of Grover Cleveland, which ordered flags at half-staff for thirty days.
